newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST-UK unemployment to fall again in October.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-UK unemployment to fall again in October.

text.p: UK unemployment is expected to have fallen by around 25,000 in October after a sharp 35,600 drop in September, economists said on Tuesday.
The Reuters consensus forecast for data due on Wednesday is for a drop of 25,000 in unemployment, while average earnings are seen rising 4.0 percent, unchanged from the September rate.
Economists said the decline in unemployment has not affected average earnings so far, but rising wage pressures would certainly be seen next year as the labour market tightens strongly.

"If we did see the unemployment rate continue to decline then people are going to talk about unemployment below the natural rate and that is going to put upward pressure on wages," said Union Plc economist Philip Uglow.
Ciaran Barr, economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said this month's report is unlikely to be anywhere near as good as September's.
The sharp decline in September was unlikely to be representative of the true pace of decline, but the underlying trend had still risen, he said.
Barr said the UK labour market was generally in good shape and getting tighter, as reflected in the rise in vacancy figures in recent months to levels last seen in 1988.
Unemployment, which was 2.073 million in September, is expected to fall below the two million mark early next year, he added.
Uglow said October's figures would continue to be boosted by the government's "benefits hotline," established to encourage people to report those claiming benefits while working.
"The fraud hotline probably fuelled the decline of September's figures...and their effects are expected in these figures too," Uglow said. "But I don't think that's the trend rate."
Analysts said the underlying trend rate decline had accelerated to 15-20,000 this year and expected this pattern to continue over the next few months.
Michael Saunders of Salomon Brothers said the recent drop in the jobless total exaggerates the trend.
"Business surveys suggest that job prospects are improving, but not quite as rapidly as the recent drop in the jobless count suggests," he said.
Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC markets, said the Labour Force Survey showed over 90 percent of jobs created in the last year were part-time
"This higher unemployment consists mainly of part-time work, obscuring the decline in full time posts as large scale redundancies continue," he added.
Unit wage cost data, also due on Wednesday, are forecast to shows a rise of 4.5 percent in the three months to September compared with a year earlier, unchanged from the August rate.
